C8.1: Play bass lines and leads where each new note cleanly takes over from the last, and overlapped notes can flow on without restarting.
C8.2: Slide a bass from one note into the next, from a small scoop to a long siren, and pick which notes slide.
C8.3: Perform a sound by hand as you play: bend a note upwards, open the filter, or fade vibrato in on a long held lead.
CT.1: Decide whether each bass note swells in or strikes hard, and get a sharp front that does not click.
CT.2: Make your own kick from scratch, with a knock at the front and a low thump, settling on the key you play.
CT.3: Shape one kick into a soft thud for a mellow tune, a hard knock for a heavy one, or a falling zap.
CT.4: Mark the start of a new section with a long falling tone you can feel, landing on the note you choose.
CT.5: Give every note of a bass line its own bright front and clean end, so a run of notes hits as separate strikes, not a drone.
CT.6: Sharpen the start of a bass note with a tiny dip in pitch that reads as attack, not as a swoop.
CT.C: Compare your kick or bass hit with one you admire and hear whether the start, the pitch fall or the body is different.
C2.8: Lifting one band is how you give a bass a vowel or pull a lead forward without thinning anything else out.
C2.9: Joining two filters lets you carve a telephone band or scoop the middle of a pad, shapes one filter alone cannot make.
C1.10: A thick, bent second oscillator beside a plain first one is the starting point for wide leads and heavy layered basses.
C7.7: Choosing where distortion, EQ and reverb sit decides whether a patch ends up clear or muddy, before you touch a single knob.
C5M.17: Closing a sound to a narrow band on one knob gives you the filtered breakdown effect heard before a drop.
C5M.18: Going from one tight voice to a wide crowd on a single knob lets a lead or bass open up exactly when the track needs it.
C5M.19: A sliding emphasised band is what makes basses seem to speak, and here it sits under one finger.
C5M.20: Roughening the wave and the output together gives you grit you can dial from clean to broken in the middle of a phrase.
C5M.21: Folding with a filter riding against it turns a plain tone into bell and metal colours without the painful top.
C6.6: Three more ways to roughen or brighten a plain wave at the source give you new raw material before any filter or effect.
C1.11: Knowing how older digital and analogue machines shaped their waves gives you their tone colours to reach for in your own patches.
CT.7: Tone plus noise is the recipe behind snares, claps and rimshots, so you can build drum hits that fit your track exactly.
CT.8: A long, low boom under the first beat of a section is one of the simplest ways to make an arrival feel huge.
CT.9: A bright snap at the front of each note is what lets a heavy bassline be heard as a rhythm and not just a rumble.
CT.10: Giving a sub some harmonics means your bass survives on phones and laptops as well as on a big system.
CT.11: A riser you built yourself can be tuned in length and pitch to lead straight into the hit it is announcing.
CT.12: Pluck, stab and growl are three of the most used bass shapes, and you can now get all three from one starting sound.
CN.1: Semitones and octaves are the ruler every tuning, bassline and melody is measured with, in any synth or music program.
CN.2: Hearing a fifth or a third on sight lets you stack oscillators and write basslines that sit well against a melody.
CN.3: Major and minor chords are the building blocks of pads, stabs and progressions, and one note is all that separates them.
CN.4: A scale tells you which notes will sound right together, so your leads and basslines stop being guesswork.
CN.5: Building chords from one scale is how a whole progression is written quickly, with every chord fitting the track.
CN.6: Inversions let you move between chords smoothly, which is what makes a pad progression glide where it used to lurch.
CN.7: Four chords in a loop is enough harmony to carry a whole track, so you can spend your attention on the sound.
CN.8: Sevenths add the richer, softer colour heard in deep pads and mellow keys, with one extra finger.
C7.8: Flangers and phasers are how a static pad, bass or drum loop is made to swirl and breathe without touching the synth itself.
C5M.22: A flanger you can throw in for one bar and pull out again is a classic way to mark the end of a phrase.
C5M.23: One knob for how much a pad moves lets you keep a long section alive by riding it slowly with one hand.
C5M.24: Sinking a sound and bringing it back is one of the clearest ways to set up a breakdown and its return.
C8.4: An arpeggiator turns three held keys into a running line, a fast way to get movement and rhythm from simple chords.
CN.9: Shifting a patch by semitones lets you write in one comfortable set of keys and still land in whatever key the track is in.
C1.12: Three squares that brighten in different ways give you three different hollow basses and leads from one idea.
CN.10: Reading a staff lets you take a melody or chord chart from any book or site and put it straight under your fingers.
CN.11: Playing from the page means a written riff or progression becomes sound in minutes, ready to turn into your own patch and part.
